“Do not ask. Yesterday I seemed to see something terrible ... as if his whole future were written in his eyes. There came a look into his eyes—and I was struck with horror at once, at what that man is preparing for himself. Once or twice in my life I have seen that look on a man’s face ... showing, as it were, the fate in store for him, and that fate, alas, came to pass. I sent you to him, Alexey, because I thought your brotherly face would help him. But everything, and all our fates, come from the Lord. ‘Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone; but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.’ Remember that. As for you, Alexey, many times I have blessed you silently because of your face. Know that,” added the elder, with a gentle smile. “This is what I think of you. You will leave these walls, but you will live in the world like a monk. You will have many enemies, yet even your enemies will love you. Life will bring you many misfortunes, but in them you will find your happiness, and you will bless life and make others bless it, which is what matters most. Well, that is your character. Fathers and teachers,” he said to his friends with a tender smile, “until today I have never told even him why this young man’s face is so dear to me. Now I will tell you. His face has been for me a remembrance and a prophecy together. When I was a child, at the dawn of my life, I had an elder brother who died before my eyes at the age of seventeen. As my life went on, I gradually came to believe that this brother was meant as a guide and a sign from above for me. Had he not entered my life, I should never have become a monk and set foot on this precious path, or so I think. He appeared to me first in my childhood, and now, at the end of my pilgrimage, it seems he has come to me a second time. It is marvelous, fathers and teachers. Alexey bears some resemblance to him in face, though not a great one. But in spirit he seems to me so like him that many times I have taken him for that young man, my brother, come back to me mysteriously at the end of my journey to remind and inspire me. I was truly amazed at so strange a fancy in myself. Do you hear this, Porfiry?” He turned to the novice who attended him. “Many times I have seen a look of mortification in your face, because I love Alexey more than you. Now you know the reason. But I love you too, know that, and many times I was grieved by your mortification. Dear friends, I want to tell you about that youth, my brother, for no one who has been in my life was more precious, more full of meaning, or more touching. My heart is full of tenderness, and at this moment I look at my whole life as though I were living it over again.”

Beloved fathers and teachers, I was born in a remote northern province, in the town of V. My father was a gentleman by birth, but he had no great standing or rank. He died when I was two years old, and I have no memory of him at all. He left my mother a small house built of wood and a modest fortune, but enough to keep her and her children comfortably. There were two of us, my elder brother Markel and I. He was eight years older than I was. He had a hasty, irritable temper, but he was kind-hearted and never ironic. He was remarkably silent, especially at home, with me, with his mother and with the servants. He did well at school but could not get along with his schoolmates, though he never quarreled with them, or so my mother has told me. Six months before his death, when he was seventeen, he became friends with a political exile. This man had been sent from Moscow to our town for freethinking, and he lived there alone. He was a fine scholar who had distinguished himself in philosophy at the university. Something drew him to Markel, and he often asked him to visit. That winter the young man spent whole evenings with him, until the exile was called to Petersburg to take up his post again, at his own request, since he had powerful friends.
